summary: Describes scenarios and simulation results for using a Path Computation Element (PCE) to add central control to a native IP network. The approach, called Centralized Control Dynamic Routing (CCDR), mixes distributed routing protocols with a central controller to give end-to-end performance guarantees across one or many domains.

eli5.summary: A traffic app picks routes for cars while each road still has its own signs. Here a central helper suggests good routes for network traffic, and this paper tests how well that works.

subtitle: Using a central path-computation controller to optimize routing in native IP networks

tldr.problem: Service provider networks using traditional distributed routing protocols (like OSPF) have limited ability to optimize end-to-end paths, handle cross-domain traffic engineering, or adapt dynamically to changing link conditions and congestion.
tldr.mechanism: Centralized Control Dynamic Routing (CCDR) adds a central controller running the Path Computation Element (PCE) to compute optimal paths based on network topology, real-time link utilization, and application requirements, while routers continue using distributed protocols for reachability.
tldr.outcome: Simulation results show CCDR can dramatically reduce congestion (average link utilization increase drops from over 30% to under 5%) and eliminate temporal congestion across complex multi-domain network topologies without requiring changes to the underlying IP infrastructure.

facts.label: Congestion elimination
facts.value: From ~20% to <3% average for congested links

today: RFC 8735 is an Informational document published in February 2020 describing simulation results and concepts for CCDR. It has not been obsoleted. This RFC serves as the foundation for related documents on protocol extensions and solution architectures for native IP path computation.

sections.title: The Problem with Distributed Routing
sections.content: Service provider networks use distributed routing protocols such as OSPF or IS-IS to calculate paths to destinations. These protocols are robust but struggle with end-to-end performance assurance, traffic engineering, and maximizing link utilization. MPLS-TE and Segment Routing provide some solutions but introduce complexity and have limited deployment for cross-domain scenarios. This document describes a simpler alternative: Centralized Control Dynamic Routing (CCDR), which combines distributed routing protocols with a central controller.
sections.eli5: Each router decides its own best path using simple rules. But sometimes a central planner looking at the whole picture could do better.

sections.title: How CCDR Works
sections.content:
CCDR uses a Path Computation Element (PCE) as a central controller. The PCE collects the network topology (via RFC 7752 BGP-LS), monitors real-time link utilization from network management systems, and knows which BGP prefixes are advertised by each router. When a new flow needs routing, the PCE computes an optimal path considering both link costs and current congestion, then tells the routers which address to use as the next hop. The routers forward traffic along this path using their normal lookup procedures, with no changes to the underlying data plane.

This approach works equally well within a single domain and across multiple domains, making it a universal solution for various network topologies and scenarios.
sections.eli5: A central planner watches the network, sees which roads are crowded, and tells routers which address to use. The routers still forward packets the same way.

sections.title: Real-World Scenarios
sections.content: The RFC describes several scenarios where CCDR adds value. In hybrid cloud deployments, an application can request end-to-end QoS guarantees, and the PCE computes a path that meets those requirements. In metro networks with tidal traffic patterns, CCDR balances load across central trunk links by routing some flows over longer paths that are underutilized. In multi-domain networks, CCDR handles the asymmetric link utilization that distributed protocols cannot fix. For temporal congestion (predictable traffic spikes), CCDR can preemptively schedule flows away from expected congestion points.
sections.eli5: A cloud company wants guaranteed quality for video calls. A city network has busy and quiet times of day. A large network spans many operator regions. All these can use CCDR to route traffic smarter.

sections.title: Simulation Results and Performance
sections.content: Simulations on realistic topologies (100 core routers and 400 edge routers) demonstrate CCDR's benefits. When new flows arrive, OSPF causes an average link utilization increase (UID) of over 30%, whereas CCDR reduces this to under 5%. For congestion elimination, before CCDR the average congestion degree (CD) on overloaded links is about 20%; after CCDR processes the same traffic, only 12 links exceed the threshold out of 20,000 total, with all exceeding links having CD under 3%. These results suggest real-world deployments will experience similar dramatic improvements.
sections.eli5: In tests, the smart controller reduces congestion from very bad to almost none, by spreading traffic better across the network.

sections.title: Deployment and Implementation
sections.content: Deploying CCDR requires the PCE to collect network topology (ideally via BGP-LS) and traffic information periodically from the network management platform. The PCE can compute optimal paths within seconds, allowing it to respond to network changes within minutes. For more agile scenarios, operators can increase sampling rates and decrease detection intervals. The approach works the same for intra-domain and inter-domain scenarios, and requires no changes to the underlying network infrastructure, making it easy to deploy and scale.
sections.eli5: The PCE watches the network every minute and tells routers which paths to use. It takes a few seconds to figure out the best paths.

sections.title: Security and Fallback
sections.content: The central control creates a single point that must be protected from attacks. Communication between the PCE and routers should be secured, and priority of control instructions needs careful design. If communication is disrupted, routers should revert to distributed protocol control. The RFC notes that RFC 5440 and RFC 8253 provide additional security information for PCE deployments.
sections.eli5: The controller is a target for attacks, so it needs protection. If it stops talking to routers, the routers go back to choosing their own routes.
